person.name: Bea Santiago
person.traits: Answered a customer-service advertisement and found herself reading scripts. Stayed because the pay was real and the rent was due. Will defend the job until she sees what it did to someone she knows.

evidence.label: Training Card
evidence.description: A laminated card from her first week: STEP 4 - ASK THE CUSTOMER TO INSTALL THE SUPPORT TOOL AND READ YOU THE SESSION CODE. IF THEY HESITATE, SAY THE TECHNICIAN IS ALREADY CONNECTED.
evidence.tactic: Handing over the controls: the 'support tool' is remote access, and the session code is the customer unlocking their own machine for a stranger.

evidence.label: Floor Badge
evidence.description: Her building pass: a photo, an operator number, 4F.

hesitant_intro.prompt: Bea opens the boarding-house door the width of her face. "I can't talk about work. It's in the contract." She looks past you down the road, the way people do when they are deciding whether they have been seen. "Sorry. I've got a shift."

choices.text: I'll come back when I can show you why it matters.

end_partial_hesitant.prompt: Bea is not going to risk the job for someone she has no reason to trust. Standing with the other witnesses first might change that.

intro.prompt: Bea lets you into a room with a mattress, a rice cooker and a headset on the windowsill. "You're the one asking about the calls. People at work talked about you." She sits on the mattress with her hoodie sleeves over her hands. "I do customer service. That's all I'm going to say about it."

choices.text: Then tell me about customer service. How did you get the job?
You're not who I'm here for. I want the people who put the script in your hand.
You read scripts to strangers until they hand over their bank details. Start there.

reassure.prompt: She watches you for a moment to see if it is a trick. "Nobody at work says script. They say call flow." A small, tired laugh. "Okay. Ask."

choices.text: How did you get the job?

press_her.prompt: "I read what they give me." Her voice goes flat. "I read it to people who called a number because a pop-up told them to. I don't dial anyone." She pulls the sleeves further down. "You want to arrest someone, there are forty of us."

choices.text: That was out of line. You're on the list of people they used, not the list I'm building.
Then tell me how you ended up as one of the forty.

ask_job.prompt: "An ad. Customer service, no experience, training provided." She says it like a line she has heard herself say before. "I messaged, they replied in about five minutes, I did a chat interview and a typing test. Then two days of training with the cards." She nods at the windowsill. "They said it was tech support. It [i]is[/i] tech support, sort of. People call in with a virus warning and we walk them through the fix."

choices.text: Show me one of the cards.

ask_job_cold.prompt: "An ad. Chat interview. Two days of training with the cards." Short, and not looking at you. "Tech support. People call in about a virus and we walk them through it."

tactic_quiz.setup: She takes a laminated card off the windowsill. The first line, in capitals: [i]STEP 1 - READ THE GREETING EXACTLY AS PRINTED. DO NOT IMPROVISE. DO NOT ANSWER QUESTIONS THAT ARE NOT ON THE CARD.[/i]
tactic_quiz.tactic: The same call, more than once
tactic_quiz.question: Why does the card forbid her from improvising?

milestone.title: Tactic Identified: The Call Flow
milestone.detail: Recognized that an operator forbidden to improvise is reading a script tuned on thousands of calls - the caller is not in a conversation, they are in a process, and the process has an answer for every hesitation.

options.text: Because the call has to be identical for everyone - it's a script tuned on thousands of people, not a conversation.
options.feedback: A script is a machine for producing one outcome. Every objection a caller might raise has been heard before and has a printed answer; a new operator improvising would break it. That is also why the same call turns up word for word at door after door - and why the moment a caller says something that is not on the card, the voice on the line gets less sure.

options.text: Because new operators make mistakes and the company wants quality.
options.feedback: That is what she was told, and it is half true - the company does want every call the same. But real support lets an agent answer a question that is not on the card. A card that forbids questions is protecting the script from the caller, not the caller from the agent.

options.text: Because the calls are recorded for legal reasons.
options.feedback: Nothing on the card is about recording, and a floor like this records nothing it can avoid. The rule is there because the words are the product - the exact wording has been tested, and an operator's own words have not.

options.text: Because she isn't technical enough to answer real questions.
options.feedback: Neither is anyone else on the floor, and it does not matter, because there is no real problem to fix. The card does not need her to know anything. It needs her to say the next line.

ask_evidence.prompt: Bea puts the card face down on the mattress. "It's a job. I know what you think it is." She looks at the headset. "The pay is real. The rent is real. Everyone I know from college is still sending applications."
ask_evidence.evidence_hint: She will defend the job until she sees what the job did to someone she knows. You need the other end of the advertisement she answered.

accepts_evidence.response: She reads the name before she reads anything else. "Trish." And then the rest, slowly, and then again. "Two and a half thousand. She paid them two and a half thousand and they - " She stops. "Same ad. Same HR. Same [i]week.[/i] I got the job and she got a receipt." The sleeves come off her hands.
"That's mine. Step four." She does not take it back. It is what she reads; it is not, yet, a reason to stop.
"It's a badge. Everyone has one." It proves where she works, which she has not denied, and nothing about why she should talk.

choices.text: What do they pay you, and how?
That's enough for now. Thank you.

press_pay.prompt: "Cash. Fridays. An envelope with my operator number on it." She says it before she can decide not to. "No payslip. I asked once and the floor lead said the accounts department was upstairs and I didn't need to worry about it." A pause. "Upstairs is where the director sits. Ocampo. Nobody goes up unless they're called."

choices.text: Let me show you something from the other end of that advertisement.
That's enough for now. Thank you.

turned.prompt: Bea sits with the statement in her lap for a long time. "There's a folder upstairs. Recruitment. It's the same ad, every month, and the ones who pay the fee never get called back, and the ones who don't get a chat interview." She looks at the headset on the windowsill as if it belongs to someone else. "I'll say that. To whoever you need me to say it to. Write it down before I change my mind."

milestone.title: Witness Turned: The Recruit
milestone.detail: Bea Santiago, hired off the advertisement that scammed her batch-mate, agreed to describe the floor above - the recruitment folder, the director who sits upstairs, the envelope with no payslip.

choices.text: You've just given me the second floor. Thank you.

end_turned.prompt: Bea's account - the advertisement, the chat interview, the training cards, the cash on Fridays and the director upstairs - is the first word from inside the fourth floor. The building has a second door now.

end_partial.prompt: You have Bea's account of the job, and she is still calling it a job. Nothing yet ties her to the floor above, or her to you.

end_shutdown.prompt: Bea stands and picks the headset off the windowsill. "I've got a shift." At the door she stops without turning round. "Don't come back here. They'll know." You will not find her at the boarding house again, and the folder upstairs stays upstairs.

milestone.title: Witness Lost: The Recruit
milestone.detail: Bea Santiago went back to work. The people an operation recruits are the ones who could describe it from inside - and the ones with the most to lose by doing so.
